details:
**Abraham's sacrifice of Isaac**
The central subject of the book. Kierkegaard examines the story in Genesis 22, where God commands Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac on Mount Moriah, and he asks how Abraham's willingness to obey can be seen as faith rather than murder.

**Teleological suspension of the ethical**
The subject of the first of the book's three "Problemata": can the ethical, meaning universal moral duty, be set aside for a higher purpose (telos)? Kierkegaard suggests that in faith, the individual's relationship to God can rise above the ethical, so the religious sphere lies beyond the ethical.

**Knight of faith**
Kierkegaard's ideal figure, represented by Abraham. Having given up everything, the knight of faith believes "by virtue of the absurd" that he will get it all back in this life. Kierkegaard says such a knight might outwardly look like an ordinary shopkeeper or tax collector.

**Knight of infinite resignation**
The figure one step below the knight of faith, who gives up a finite thing they love, such as a beloved, and finds peace in that eternal loss but does not expect to get it back. Kierkegaard says he himself can make this movement but cannot make the movement of faith.

**Johannes de Silentio**
The pseudonym under which Kierkegaard published Fear and Trembling in 1843. The narrator repeatedly says he cannot understand Abraham and that faith, which embraces the absurd, is beyond him.

**The three Problemata**
The book's three central questions: whether there is a teleological suspension of the ethical, whether there is an absolute duty to God, and whether Abraham was ethically justified in hiding his purpose from Sarah, Eliezer, and Isaac.

**Agamemnon at Aulis and the tragic hero**
Kierkegaard contrasts Abraham with Agamemnon, who sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia for the sake of the Greek army. Agamemnon is a "tragic hero" because he acts for a higher ethical good that others can understand and sympathize with, while Abraham acts alone and in silence, beyond the ethical.

**Agnes and the Merman**
A Danish legend that Kierkegaard retells in Problema III. A merman sets out to seduce the innocent Agnes but is moved by her trust in him, and Kierkegaard uses the story to explore concealment, the demonic, and repentance.

**Regine Olsen**
Kierkegaard's former fiancée, whom he broke off his engagement with in 1841. Many readers see his own sacrifice of her behind the book's themes of resignation and faith.

**Repetition**
Another Kierkegaard book, published on the same day as Fear and Trembling (October 16, 1843) under the pseudonym Constantin Constantius.

**Jacques Derrida's The Gift of Death**
A work in which Derrida reads Fear and Trembling and introduces the formula "every other is wholly other" (tout autre est tout autre). He argues that any responsibility to one person sacrifices our responsibility to all others.

**The "Exordium" and its variations**
The book opens with a section, sometimes translated "Tuning Up," that imagines several different versions of Abraham's journey to Moriah, followed by a "Eulogy on Abraham" praising him as the father of faith.

**The "absolute duty to God"**
The subject of Problema II. Kierkegaard asks whether a person can owe God a duty that outranks every ethical duty, and he connects it to the idea of the "single individual" who stands in a private relationship to God.
